name: Puṇḍalīka
summary: The devotee of Paṇḍharpūr whose service to his parents brought Kṛṣṇa to his door; asked to wait, the Lord stood on the brick Puṇḍalīka tossed him and remains there as Viṭṭhala. Vārkarīs chant 'Puṇḍalīka varade Hari Viṭṭhala'.

realization_account.text: Kṛṣṇa himself came to see him because of his devotion to his parents.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Viṭṭhalpant
summary: Father of Nivṛttināth, Jñāneśvar, Sopāndev and Muktābāī: a brahmin of Āpegāv who took sannyāsa at Kāśī, returned to household life at his guru's command, and was outcast with his family; he and his wife Rukmiṇībāī are said to have given up their lives at Prayāga as expiation so that their children might be accepted.
notes: Name of his sannyāsa-guru differs between accounts (some say Rāmānanda / Śrīpād); not recorded here.

name: Gahinīnāth
summary: Nāth yogī, disciple of Gorakṣanātha, who initiated Nivṛttināth in a cave on the Brahmagiri near Tryambakeśvar and charged him to spread devotion to Kṛṣṇa; through him the Vārkarī saints trace their Nāth initiation.

name: Nivṛttināth
summary: Eldest of the four sibling-saints and Jñāneśvar's guru; initiated into the Nāth path by Gahinīnāth, he passed it to Jñāneśvar and bade him write the Jñāneśvarī and then an independent work (Amṛtānubhava). His own abhaṅgas are few. Samādhi at Tryambakeśvar.

name: Jñāneśvar
summary: Marathi saint-philosopher (Jñānadev, Jñānobā), second of the four siblings, disciple of his brother Nivṛttināth in the Nāth line. At about fifteen he spoke the Jñāneśvarī at Nevāse (1290), then the Amṛtānubhava, the Cāṅgadeva Pāsaṣṭī, the Haripāṭh and abhaṅgas to Viṭṭhala; he founded the Vārkarī saint-tradition with Nāmdev, travelled with him, and at twenty-one entered living samādhi (sañjīvana samādhi) at Āḷandī.

realization_account.text: Realized from boyhood by his guru's grace; made a buffalo recite the Veda at Paiṭhaṇ, rode a moving wall to meet Cāṅgadev, and entered living samādhi at Āḷandī where he is believed still present.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Sopāndev
summary: Third of the four siblings, disciple of Nivṛttināth; a few abhaṅgas survive under his name; samādhi at Sāsvaḍ.

name: Muktābāī
summary: Youngest of the four siblings; her 'door' abhaṅgas (tāṭīce abhaṅga) coaxed Jñāneśvar out of the hut he had shut himself into after being insulted, teaching that the saint bears insult without anger; the yogī Cāṅgadev became her disciple. Tradition says she vanished in a flash of lightning at Mehūṇ on the Tāpī.

name: Saccidānanda Bābā
summary: Scribe who wrote down the Jñāneśvarī at Nevāse as Jñāneśvar spoke it; tradition says Jñāneśvar restored him to life.

name: Cāṅgadev (Cāṅgā Vaṭeśvar)
summary: A yogī said to have lived fourteen hundred years by yogic power, who came riding a tiger with a cobra for a whip to meet Jñāneśvar and found the siblings riding a moving wall; humbled, he took Muktābāī as guru. Jñāneśvar's Cāṅgadeva Pāsaṣṭī is addressed to him.
notes: Distinct from the Mahānubhāva Cāṅgadeva Rāüḷ of Dvārakā (tch:cangadeva-raul).

name: Nāmdev
summary: Tailor-caste (śimpī) saint of Paṇḍharpūr (c. 1270–1350), Viṭṭhala's intimate from childhood — the Lord ate his offering — who, after Gorā Kumbhār judged him 'unbaked', took Visobā Khecar as guru and learned to see God everywhere. Companion of Jñāneśvar, he vowed to 'dance in kīrtan and light the lamp of knowledge in the world', carried Viṭṭhala's name to Punjab in Hindi songs, and took samādhi at the temple step (Nāmdev pāyarī).

realization_account.text: Viṭṭhala spoke and ate with him as a child; only after taking a guru did he see the Lord in all things.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Visobā Khecar
summary: Nāmdev's guru: found resting his feet on a Śiva-liṅga (at Auṇḍhā Nāgnāth), he told Nāmdev to set them where God was not — and wherever Nāmdev moved them a liṅga appeared, teaching that God fills everything.

name: Janābāī
summary: Maidservant in Nāmdev's household (d. c. 1350) whose abhaṅgas sing of Viṭṭhala grinding, pounding and washing with her; the model of devotion within menial work.

name: Cokhāmeḷā
summary: Mahār saint of Maṅgaḷveḍhe (d. c. 1338), disciple of Nāmdev, kept outside the temple by caste but devoted to Viṭṭhala; his abhaṅgas voice both love and the pain of exclusion ('the sugarcane is crooked, its juice is not'). He died when a wall he was building collapsed; Nāmdev carried the bones, which murmured 'Viṭṭhala', to Paṇḍharpūr, where his samādhi stands before the temple's gate.

name: Soyrābāī
summary: Wife of Cokhāmeḷā, poet of abhaṅgas that question bodily impurity and celebrate oneness in devotion.

name: Karmameḷā
summary: Son of Cokhāmeḷā and Soyrābāī; a few abhaṅgas protesting caste treatment are ascribed to him.

name: Nirmaḷā
summary: Sister of Cokhāmeḷā and wife of Bankā; a few abhaṅgas.

name: Bankā
summary: Cokhāmeḷā's brother-in-law, a Mahār devotee-poet of the same circle.

name: Gorā Kumbhār
summary: Potter-saint of Terḍhokī (13th–14th c.): in ecstatic kīrtan he trampled his own child into the clay; with the stick used to test pots he judged the assembled saints and found Nāmdev 'unbaked' for lack of a guru.

name: Sāvatā Mālī
summary: Gardener-saint of Araṇ who worshipped in his vegetable plot and never went to Paṇḍharpūr — the Lord came to him; 'onion, radish and greens — all are my mother Viṭhābāī'.

name: Narahari Sonār
summary: Goldsmith of Paṇḍharpūr, a devotee of Śiva who would not look at Viṭṭhala; measuring Viṭṭhala's waist blindfolded he felt Śiva's form, and saw Hari and Hara as one.

name: Sena (Sena Nhāvī)
summary: Barber-saint. In the Marathi tradition a Vārkarī poet whose place the Lord took to shave the king while Sena was absorbed in worship; in the Bhaktamāl a barber of Bāndhavgaṛh and one of Rāmānanda's twelve disciples; a hymn under the name Sain stands in the Sikh scripture (context only).
notes: Whether the Marathi Sena and the Hindi Sena are one person is disputed; kept as one entry with both lineages.

name: Kānhopātrā
summary: Daughter of a courtesan of Maṅgaḷveḍhe (15th c.) who refused a king's summons and died at the Paṇḍharpūr temple, where she is the only saint with a memorial inside the precinct; her abhaṅgas plead for Viṭṭhala's protection.

name: Bhānudās
summary: Eknāth's great-grandfather (tradition 1448–1513), said to have brought the image of Viṭṭhala back to Paṇḍharpūr from Vijayanagara.

name: Janārdana Svāmī
summary: Eknāth's guru (tradition 1504–1575), an official at the Devagiri (Daulatābād) fort and devotee of Dattātreya, through whom Eknāth received Datta's vision; Eknāth signs his verses 'Ekā Janārdanī'.

name: Eknāth
summary: Brahmin saint of Paiṭhaṇ (1533–1599), disciple of Janārdana Svāmī: corrected the Jñāneśvarī text (1584), wrote the Eknāthī Bhāgavat, the Bhāvārtha Rāmāyaṇa, bhāruḍs and abhaṅgas, and lived as a householder of legendary patience — bathing again and again without anger when spat upon, pouring Gaṅgā water meant for Rāmeśvaram into a dying donkey's mouth, feeding Mahārs at his ancestors' rite. Kṛṣṇa is said to have served in his house as Śrīkhaṇḍyā.

realization_account.text: Received Datta's vision through Janārdana's grace; Kṛṣṇa served him as a household servant for twelve years.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Gāvbā
summary: Disciple of Eknāth credited with completing the Bhāvārtha Rāmāyaṇa after Eknāth's death.

name: Tukārām
summary: Kuṇbī grocer of Dehu (1608–1650 by the usual tradition) who, ruined by famine and bereavement, turned wholly to Viṭṭhala; initiated in a dream by Bābājī Caitanya with the mantra 'Rāma Kṛṣṇa Hari'. His abhaṅgas — thrown into the Indrāyaṇī at the order of the brahmin Rāmeśvar Bhaṭṭ and restored after thirteen days — became the Tukārām Gāthā. He is 'the pinnacle' of the Vārkarī temple; tradition says he departed bodily for Vaikuṇṭha (Tukārām Bīj).

tradition.text: 1608–1650 (Śaka 1530–1571); some accounts give 1598 for his birth

realization_account.text: Initiated in a dream; Viṭṭhala restored his drowned abhaṅgas; at the end he ascended to Vaikuṇṭha in his body.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Bābājī Caitanya
summary: The guru who initiated Tukārām in a dream, giving the mantra 'Rāma Kṛṣṇa Hari'; Tukārām names his line through Rāghava Caitanya and Keśava Caitanya.

name: Rāmeśvar Bhaṭṭ
summary: Brahmin of Vāgholī who condemned a Kuṇbī's expounding of scripture and ordered Tukārām's notebooks sunk; after their restoration he became Tukārām's disciple.

name: Santājī Jagnāḍe
summary: Oil-presser (Telī) companion of Tukārām who wrote down his abhaṅgas and sang with him.

name: Bahiṇābāī
summary: Brahmin woman saint (1628–1700) who took Tukārām as guru in a dream, bore her husband's anger, and wrote an autobiography in abhaṅgas and the image of the saints as one temple with Tukārām its pinnacle.

name: Niḷobā
summary: 17th–18th c. Vārkarī poet of Pimpaḷner who received Tukārām's grace in a dream after Tukārām's departure; regarded as Tukārām's spiritual successor in one line.

name: Mahīpati
summary: Brahmin hagiographer of Tāharābād (1715–1790), author of the Bhaktavijaya, Santalīlāmṛta and Bhaktalīlāmṛta, through which the Vārkarī saints' lives are told.

name: Gāḍge Mahārāj
summary: Wandering kīrtankār and reformer (1876–1956) who used Vārkarī kīrtan and the chant 'Gopālā Gopālā Devakīnandan Gopālā' to preach cleanliness, education and the end of caste discrimination and animal sacrifice.

name: Tukaḍojī Mahārāj
summary: Vidarbha kīrtankār and bhajan poet (1909–1968), author of the Grāmgītā on village uplift through devotion.

name: Viṣṇubuvā Jog (Jog Mahārāj)
summary: Vārkarī teacher (d. 1920) who founded the Vārkarī Śikṣaṇ Saṃsthā at Āḷandī (1917) to train kīrtankārs in the Jñāneśvarī and the saints' texts.

name: Rāmānanda
summary: Founder of the Rāmānandī sampradāya, teacher at Vārāṇasī (Pañcagaṅgā ghāṭ). By one tradition a disciple of Rāghavānanda in Rāmānuja's line who founded his own order after being faulted over commensality; by the independent Rāmānandī account, the founder of an order descending from Rāma himself. He taught devotion to Rāma with Sītā through the Rāma mantra, used the vernacular, and — so the Bhaktamāl says — initiated twelve disciples including a weaver (Kabīr), a cobbler (Raidās), a barber (Sena), a Jāṭ farmer (Dhanna), a Rajput king (Pīpā) and women (Padmāvatī, Surasurī).

name: Rāghavānanda
summary: Rāmānanda's guru in the older Rāmānandī lineage lists, placed in the line descending from Rāmānuja.

name: Anantānanda
summary: One of Rāmānanda's twelve disciples, through whom the Galtā line (Kṛṣṇadās Payahārī) descends.

name: Sukhānanda
summary: One of Rāmānanda's twelve disciples named in the Bhaktamāl.

name: Surasurānanda
summary: One of Rāmānanda's twelve disciples; the Vaiṣṇavamatābjabhāskara is framed as Rāmānanda's answers to his questions.

name: Naraharyānanda
summary: One of Rāmānanda's twelve disciples named in the Bhaktamāl; sometimes confused with Tulsīdās's guru Narharidās.

name: Bhāvānanda
summary: One of Rāmānanda's twelve disciples named in the Bhaktamāl.

name: Surasurī
summary: Wife of Surasurānanda, counted among Rāmānanda's twelve disciples in the Bhaktamāl.

name: Padmāvatī
summary: Woman disciple of Rāmānanda named among the twelve in the Bhaktamāl.

name: Pīpā
summary: Rajput king of Gāgraun who renounced his throne to become Rāmānanda's disciple and wandered with his wife Sītā; a hymn of his stands in the Sikh scripture (context).

name: Dhannā
summary: Jāṭ farmer of Rajasthan whose simple faith made God eat his offering and tend his field; counted Rāmānanda's disciple in the Bhaktamāl; hymns in the Sikh scripture (context).

name: Kṛṣṇadās Payahārī
summary: Rāmānandī ascetic ('who lives on milk'), disciple of Anantānanda, who established the seat at Galtā near Jaipur — by tradition after defeating the Nāth yogīs there; guru of Agradās and Kīlhadās.

name: Agradās
summary: Disciple of Kṛṣṇadās Payahārī, seated at Raivāsā (16th c.), founder of the rasik mode of Rāma devotion and guru of Nābhādās, whom he commanded to write the Bhaktamāl.

name: Kīlhadās
summary: Disciple of Kṛṣṇadās Payahārī who succeeded at Galtā; associated with the ascetic and yogic (tapasvī) branch.

name: Nābhādās
summary: Author of the Bhaktamāl (c. 1600), raised as an abandoned child by Agradās and Kīlhadās at Galtā; his garland of devotees crosses sect and caste.

name: Priyādās
summary: Vṛndāvana poet who wrote the Bhaktirasabodhinī (1712), the commentary that turned the Bhaktamāl's allusions into the standard stories of the saints.

name: Narharidās
summary: Tulsīdās's guru, from whom he heard the Rāma story as a boy at Sūkarakhet (Mānas 1.30); the Mānas's opening salutation to the guru as 'Hari in human form' (nara-rūpa hari) is read as a pun on his name.

name: Tulsīdās
summary: Poet-saint of Rāma (c. 1532–1623; tradition 1497–1623), a brahmin abandoned at birth and raised by sādhus, disciple of Narharidās. Turned to Rāma, by tradition, by his wife Ratnāvalī's rebuke, he lived at Ayodhyā, Citrakūṭ and Vārāṇasī (Assi ghāṭ), where Hanumān led him to the vision of Rāma. He wrote the Rāmcaritmānas (from 1574), the Vinaya Patrikā, Kavitāvalī, Gītāvalī, Dohāvalī and other works; the Hanumān Cālīsā is traditionally his. The Bhaktamāl calls him Vālmīki reborn for the Kali age.

realization_account.text: Hanumān, met through a ghost's guidance, showed him Rāma at Citrakūṭ; Śiva approved the Mānas at Vārāṇasī.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Hita Harivaṃśa
summary: Founder of the Rādhāvallabha sampradāya (tradition 1502–1552), born at Bād near Mathurā, who received his mantra from Rādhā herself, settled in Vṛndāvana and installed Rādhāvallabha (1535). Author of the Hita Caurāsī and, by his tradition's account, the Rādhā-sudhānidhi; the tradition regards him as the flute of Kṛṣṇa incarnate.

realization_account.text: Rādhā gave him the mantra in a dream (or vision); he is Kṛṣṇa's flute (vaṃśī) incarnate.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Vanacandra
summary: Hita Harivaṃśa's son and successor at the Rādhāvallabha temple.

name: Sevak (Dāmodardās)
summary: Early disciple-poet of the Rādhāvallabha tradition (16th c.), whose Sevak Vāṇī praises Hita Harivaṃśa and the doctrine of hita.

name: Dhruvadās
summary: Rādhāvallabha poet-theologian (late 16th – 17th c.), author of the forty-two līlās (Bayālīs Līlā).

name: Harirām Vyās
summary: Sanāḍhya brahmin of Orchhā (16th c.) who settled in Vṛndāvana; a poet of the pair's love associated with Hita Harivaṃśa (his affiliation is also claimed by other sampradāyas).

name: Prabodhānanda Sarasvatī
summary: Gauḍīya ascetic poet of Vṛndāvana to whom the Gauḍīyas ascribe the Rādhā-sudhānidhi (disputed with the Rādhāvallabhīs).

name: Svāmī Haridās
summary: Singer-saint of Vṛndāvana (16th c.), founder of the Haridāsī (Sakhī) sampradāya, who sang the eternal pair's play in the Kelimāl; at his singing in Nidhivan the image of Bāṅke Bihārī appeared. Revered as Tānsen's teacher; the Emperor Akbar is said to have visited him in disguise to hear him. His tradition holds him to be the sakhī Lalitā.

realization_account.text: Bāṅke Bihārī manifested before him; he is Lalitā sakhī.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The guru Āśudhīra is given in the Nimbārkī account; the independent Haridāsī account differs.

name: Āśudhīra
summary: Named as Svāmī Haridās's guru in the account that places the Haridāsīs within the Nimbārka sampradāya.

name: Tānsen
summary: Court musician of Akbar (d. 1589), remembered as Svāmī Haridās's disciple in dhrupad.

name: Viṭṭhal Vipul
summary: Successor of Svāmī Haridās in the ascetic line.

name: Bihārinidev
summary: Ācārya of the ascetic Haridāsī line (late 16th – 17th c.), author of doctrinal verses (siddhānta) of the sampradāya.

name: Mīrābāī
summary: Rajput princess of Meṛtā (tradition c. 1498–1547), married into the Sisodia house of Mewar and early widowed, who took Kṛṣṇa as Giridhar Gopāl for her husband, danced with sādhus, survived the poison and the snake sent by the Rāṇā, went to Vṛndāvana and then Dvārakā, and — so tradition says — merged into the image of Raṇchoḍ. The Bhaktamāl praises her for casting off family honour; songs in her name name Raidās as guru.

realization_account.text: Merged bodily into Kṛṣṇa's image at Dvārakā.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Raidās as guru is the songs' claim; chronology makes a direct meeting doubtful.

name: Cakradhar Svāmī
summary: Founder of the Mahānubhāva panth (13th c.), held by his followers to be Parameśvara's fifth incarnation. By their account the Gujarati prince Haripāla of Bharuch died and Cāṅgadeva Rāüḷ entered his body; receiving Govindaprabhu's grace at Ṛddhipur, he wandered Maharashtra teaching in Marathi, admitted women and all castes to renunciation, forbade the worship of the devatās, and, threatened by the Yādava court, departed to the north (c. 1274).

tradition.text: incarnation of Parameśvara; left for the north Śaka 1196 (1274)

realization_account.text: Parameśvara himself, one of the five Kṛṣṇas; entered the dead body of Haripāla; survived the executioner and left for the north.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Govindaprabhu (Guṇḍam Rāüḷ)
summary: The 'mad' saint of Ṛddhipur (13th c.), Cakradhar's guru and the fourth of the five Kṛṣṇas; his child-like, unconventional acts are read as divine play.

name: Cāṅgadeva Rāüḷ
summary: Saint of Dvārakā counted third of the five Kṛṣṇas; by Mahānubhāva tradition his spirit entered the dead prince Haripāla, who became Cakradhar.
notes: Distinct from the Vārkarī yogī Cāṅgadev (tch:cangadeva-vatesvar).

name: Dattātreya
summary: In the Mahānubhāva reckoning, the second of the five incarnations (pañca-kṛṣṇa) of Parameśvara, eternally present at Māhūr, whose grace descends to the later incarnations.

name: Nāgadevācārya (Bhaṭobās)
summary: Cakradhar's chosen successor (d. c. 1312), who held the community together after Cakradhar's departure and approved the compilation of the Līḷācaritra.

name: Mhāimbhaṭ
summary: Disciple who gathered the eyewitness memories of Cakradhar into the Līḷācaritra (c. 1278) and compiled the Govindaprabhu-caritra.

name: Keśobās (Keśirāja Vyās)
summary: Disciple who arranged Cakradhar's sayings in the Sūtrapāṭh and his parables in the Dṛṣṭāntapāṭh.

name: Mahadaisā (Mahadamba)
summary: Woman disciple of Cakradhar and Govindaprabhu, remembered for her questions in the Līḷācaritra and for the Dhavaḷe, among the earliest Marathi songs by a woman.

name: Bāïsā
summary: Woman disciple who cared for Cakradhar; figures often in the Līḷācaritra.

name: Narendra
summary: Mahānubhāva poet (late 13th – 14th c.), author of one of the seven classic Mahānubhāva poems.

name: Bhāskarabhaṭṭa Borīkar
summary: Mahānubhāva poet (early 14th c.), author of two of the seven classic poems — the Śiśupāla-vadha and the Uddhava-gītā (Ekādaśa-skandha).

name: Dāmodara Paṇḍita
summary: Mahānubhāva poet (late 13th – 14th c.), author of one of the seven classic Mahānubhāva poems.

name: Ravaḷobās
summary: Mahānubhāva poet (late 13th – 14th c.), author of one of the seven classic Mahānubhāva poems.

name: Viśvanātha Bāḷāpurkar
summary: Mahānubhāva poet (late 13th – 14th c.), author of one of the seven classic Mahānubhāva poems.

name: Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍita
summary: Mahānubhāva poet (late 13th – 14th c.), author of one of the seven classic Mahānubhāva poems.

name: Hemādri (Hemāḍpant)
summary: Minister of the Yādava king Rāmacandra and author of the Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi; in Mahānubhāva memory the court's leading opponent of Cakradhar.
notes: U26 contribution: his role as opponent is the Mahānubhāva account (reported by the opposing side).

name: Śaṅkaradeva
summary: Founder of the Ekaśaraṇa Dharma (tradition 1449–1568), of the Śiromaṇi Bhuyan family of Bardowā; orphaned and raised by his grandmother, he studied under Mahendra Kandali, made two long pilgrimages, preached exclusive devotion to Kṛṣṇa through the name, converted Mādhavadeva, and — persecuted in the Ahom kingdom — continued under the Koch kings Naranārāyaṇa and Cilarāi. Poet of the Kīrtana-ghoṣā, bargīts and aṅkīyā nāṭs; called the Mahāpuruṣa.

scholarly.text: c. 1449–1568 (the traditional span of 119 years is sometimes questioned)

realization_account.text: Recognised as the Mahāpuruṣa; Assamese hagiographies tell of a meeting with Caitanya at Purī (not found in Bengali sources).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Mādhavadeva
summary: Śaṅkaradeva's chief disciple and successor (tradition 1489–1596), a Śākta until a debate with Śaṅkaradeva over a goat sacrifice converted him; lifelong celibate, poet of the Nām-ghoṣā, many bargīts, the jhumurā plays and the Assamese Bhakti-ratnāvalī.

name: Dāmodaradeva
summary: Brahmin preacher (tradition 1488–1598), founder of the Brahma saṃhati; the Mahāpuruṣīyā account makes him Śaṅkaradeva's disciple, while his own followers (Dāmodarīyā) stress his independence.

name: Harideva
summary: Brahmin associate of the early Ekaśaraṇa movement, counted with Dāmodaradeva among the founders of the Brahma saṃhati.

name: Bhaṭṭadeva (Vaikuṇṭhanātha Bhāgavata Bhaṭṭācārya)
summary: Disciple of Dāmodaradeva (1558–1638) whose Kathā-Bhāgavata and Kathā-Gītā are the foundation of Assamese prose.

name: Gopāla Ātā (Gopāladeva of Bhavānīpur)
summary: Disciple of Mādhavadeva and founder of the Kāla saṃhati (16th–17th c.).

name: Aniruddhadeva
summary: Founder of the Māyāmarā (Moāmoriyā) sattra in the Kāla saṃhati line, whose followers later rose against the Ahom state.

name: Puruṣottama Ṭhākur
summary: Grandson of Śaṅkaradeva and leader of the Puruṣa saṃhati.

name: Caturbhuja Ṭhākur
summary: Grandson of Śaṅkaradeva, with Puruṣottama a leader of the Puruṣa saṃhati.

name: Mathurādāsa Ātā
summary: Disciple of Mādhavadeva, first head (sattrādhikār) at Bārpeṭā by tradition; associated with the Nikā saṃhati.

name: Badulā Padma Ātā
summary: Disciple of Mādhavadeva counted among the founders of the Nikā saṃhati.

name: Rāmacaraṇa Ṭhākura
summary: Mādhavadeva's nephew and author of a verse Guru-carita of Śaṅkaradeva.

name: Daityāri Ṭhākura
summary: Author of a verse life of Śaṅkaradeva and Mādhavadeva.

name: Cāndsāi
summary: Muslim tailor who became Śaṅkaradeva's disciple, remembered as proof that refuge was open to all.

name: Naranārāyaṇa
summary: Koch king (r. c. 1540–1586) at whose court Śaṅkaradeva spent his last years; commissioned the Guṇamālā and defended Śaṅkaradeva against brahmin accusers.

name: Cilarāi (Śukladhvaja)
summary: Koch general, brother of Naranārāyaṇa and patron of Śaṅkaradeva, who sheltered him at court.

name: Mādhava Kandali
summary: 14th-c. poet of the first Assamese Rāmāyaṇa, honoured by Śaṅkaradeva, who completed its missing Uttarakāṇḍa (Mādhavadeva its Ādikāṇḍa).
notes: A predecessor revered by the tradition, not a member.

name: Viṣṇupurī
summary: Sannyāsī compiler of the Sanskrit Bhakti-ratnāvalī, which Mādhavadeva rendered into Assamese.
notes: Date and affiliation uncertain; claimed in both Assamese and Bengali traditions.

name: Samartha Rāmdās
summary: Marathi saint (1608–1681/82), born Nārāyaṇ Ṭhosar at Jāmb, who fled his wedding at the word 'sāvadhān' ('beware'), spent twelve years in austerity and Rāma-japa at Ṭākaḷī near Nāsik and twelve years on pilgrimage, then founded maṭhs and Māruti temples, taught the Dāsbodh and Manāce Śloka and, in Marathi tradition, guided Śivājī.

realization_account.text: Rāma and Hanumān appeared to him as a boy; Rāma initiated him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The extent of his relation to Śivājī is debated by historians.

name: Kalyāṇ Svāmī
summary: Rāmdās's principal disciple and scribe of the Dāsbodh.

name: Veṇābāī
summary: Young widow of Miraj who became Rāmdās's disciple and a mahant of the order (17th c.).

name: Narsinh Mehta
summary: Nāgar brahmin poet of Junāgaḍh (15th c.), the first great Gujarati poet: taunted by his sister-in-law, he fasted before a Śiva-liṅga in the forest until Śiva led him to see Kṛṣṇa's rāsa; thereafter he sang with low-caste devotees, and Kṛṣṇa rescued him in the Hāramālā, Māmeruṃ and Huṇḍī episodes. Author of 'Vaiṣṇava jana to'.

realization_account.text: Śiva showed him the rāsa-līlā; Kṛṣṇa placed a garland on him before the king.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Annamācārya (Tāḷḷapāka Annamayya)
summary: Telugu singer-saint of Tirumala (1408–1503 by tradition), a Śrīvaiṣṇava initiate, who composed thousands of saṅkīrtanas to Veṅkaṭeśvara preserved on copper plates.

name: Tyāgarāja
summary: Telugu singer-saint of Tiruvaiyāru (1767–1847), devotee of Rāma, composer of some seven hundred surviving kṛtis and two musical dramas; he declined the Tanjore court's patronage ('Is wealth happiness, or service near Rāma?') and is said to have taken sannyāsa before death.

name: Baḍu Caṇḍīdās
summary: Bengali poet of the Śrīkṛṣṇakīrtana; the name 'Caṇḍīdās' is shared by several poets whose lyrics Caitanya loved and the Sahajiyās later claimed.

name: Vidyāpati
summary: Maithili court poet of Mithila (c. 1352–1448) whose songs of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa (and of Śiva) Caitanya relished.

name: Bhadrācala Rāmadās (Kañcarla Gopanna)
summary: 17th-c. Telugu revenue official of Golconda who spent state revenue on the Rāma temple at Bhadrācalam, was imprisoned, and — by tradition — freed when Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa paid the sultan in gold; author of the Dāśarathi Śatakam and kīrtanas.
notes: A tradition that Kabīr initiated him is chronologically impossible; recorded only as the tradition's account.
